Chapter 1: Daivapuruṣakāra (Destiny and Human Effort).
He upon whose rising the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, blossom like a lotus, and upon whose setting they wither and close, that Sun, the abode of rays, is victorious.
"Having conquered the earth by means of a sacrifice to the Lord of Yakṣas"— thus for a king who is thus exerting himself,
there is no sin in slaying those who create obstacles, provided he slaughters the sacrificial animals in the sacrifices according to the prescribed sequence.

One who is endowed with the powers of energy, counsel, and sovereignty; who is wise, has subdued his senses and circle of servants; who is beloved by his subjects, steadfast, patient, and a servant of the elders—such a person is desired as one who seeks victory.

His astrologer should also be of such a kind: one who has lived for a year [in training], is modest in dress, wise, skilled in the independent movements of the limbs, of noble birth, dexterous, bold, free from physical defects, and well-disciplined.
Poets describe the accomplishment of results for that [action] as being composed of both divine and human effort.
Among them, some, having set aside human effort, say that divine power alone is the giver of results.
One obtains only that which is to be obtained; one goes only to that which is to be gone to;
and one experiences only those sorrows and joys that are destined to be experienced.
If success were to come from mere exertion, no one would fail to obtain the fruit;
yet people are seen emaciated by their livelihoods, struggling all day and night.

For like a bird that falls into slaughter when it alights upon a noble person who lacks power, one who is ordained by destiny cannot be advised; he is not the master of others, nor is he the master of himself.
Therefore, fate is indeed predominant; one should not perform human effort. For even in this world, one who is inactive enjoys the highest prosperity.

Those who, fickle with self-conceit, advance against their enemies while disregarding fate— which is difficult to overcome due to malice— even if they have conquered Fortune, she does not come into their grasp, for they are but great sacrificial beasts for the God of Death, even after a long time.
Likewise, others, disregarding destiny altogether, rely upon fortitude; they who perceive the accomplishment of action through direct observation proclaim effort alone as the means.
For a king who lacks exertion, even if he be possessed of intelligence,
is always to be despised by his enemies like a venomless serpent.
A man steadfast in exertion surpasses those who are merely steadfast in speech;
those who are steadfast in speech wait upon and serve him who is steadfast in exertion.
One who is dull-witted regarding the calculation of methods, whose regard for human effort is dormant,
does not kiss the face of Fortune through the labors of his desires;
for only he who possesses a single, well-ascertained policy through valor immediately [reaps] the fruit of his learning.
Hari drinks the honey from the elephant's tears, which is well-scented with rut.
The attainment of results is seen to follow the patterns of agriculture and rain;
regarding this matter, hear these verses uttered from the mouth of Dvaipāyana.
Neither the divine without the human, nor the human without the divine,
can accomplish a purpose by itself, just as fire is not produced from a single kindling stick.
All undertakings succeed through the conjunction of destiny and human effort; they never succeed through either one alone.
"The divine [fate] instructs the man here, saying 'it shall be for him'; thus it is the instructor.
Here, it will not be for me; how then can there be an unearned fruit?"
Having with effort attained human form, a man who restrains himself during the opportunity for exertion awaits the decree of fate; thus, calamities not caused by himself do not touch him.
The fruit of action acquired by a *sāttvika* person ripens with ease through energetic exertion; that of a *rājasa* person, with difficulty;
and the remainder, with great hardship. Therefore, those who act as men should seek out and distinguish [the nature of their efforts].
(Chapter 2: The Qualities of the Lunar Days)
Henceforth, having examined the opinions of the sages and calculated [the time],

those skilled in horoscopy desire to determine the time of departure once the birth of the Lord of the Earth— who is celebrated as preeminent and perfected in the weighty syllables of extensive speech— is known.
Even though it was unknown and fruitless, you spoke here of the *Ratnāvalī* as if it were an [ancient] syllable.
When the zodiacal sign of the hora has been determined, when the positional strength of the planets has been grasped,
and when the lifespan has been fully understood, then the auspicious or inauspicious fruit may be declared.
Others say that even when the time of birth is unknown,
the moment of departure is suitable for lords of men.
Vasiṣṭha spoke these words: "You are destined for success."
Whether one has not asked or has asked, for anyone who desires to go,
one should determine their auspicious or inauspicious fortune from the houses, the four angles, and the trines.
For all mortals, though they desire good or evil results through fate, are helplessly brought into the sphere of destiny by fate itself.
In the past, when he had approached Viṣṇu for the sake of knowledge,
he heard the words of the Lord of the World issuing from his lotus-like mouth.
For a person who asks about the essence [of his horoscope], the result residing in the planet and the zodiac sign—
that would be his essential birth, provided that...
It may also be in another's house.
Having understood the treatise according to the proper method, through the determination of strengths and weaknesses,
one should consider everything exactly as it was stated in the *Jātaka* here as well.
Therefore, the king, holding flowers, jewels, and the best of fruits in his hands,
should bow to the sun at dawn while standing facing the eastern direction,
[and consult] those who are skilled in the sciences of horā and aṅga and who act for his welfare.
Having dismissed the groups of divine attendants, one should ask [the question] all at once.
Then, having been questioned by the king, the astrologer, immediately upon being asked,
should infer the result through the omens of rising signs according to the perspective of the treatises;
even if it should be unfavorable, he must declare it "it is so" in the royal assembly.
It should be clearly explained to the king or to the minister.
When the ground is pleasant for walking, covered with cow dung fit for drinking,
and filled with water and flowers, the astrologer who knows the movements of the planets and constellations should predict a favorable outcome for the questioner after he has bathed.
O King, if the tips of his hands touch the openings of the ears, mouth, nose, or private parts, or the cheeks, hips, or shoulders,
the army utters auspicious sounds and subdues its enemies.

Having observed the rising sign (lagna) of one desiring to march, or its lord, or the rising sign of the enemy, or its lord, or the sign of the enemy's ascendant, or its lord— if these are situated in a house of increase (upacaya),
know that the enemy's faction has been utterly destroyed. Or else, [know it] by this [other method].
For if [the lord of the seventh house] is conjoined with the hibuka or situated in the eighth house for one who asks.
The rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*) is behind the sun, while the one to be marched against (*yātavya*) is in front of the sun;
and that which stands in the seventh position from the ally (*ākranda*)—these should be considered as equal [in strength] according to their respective power.

BY 2.15a–c: When Jupiter, Mercury, the Sun, Venus, and Saturn are situated in the fifth, fourth, third, second, eleventh, and tenth houses respectively, the querent achieves his purpose and, having quickly conquered his enemies, returns to his home.
Alternatively, if Mars and Saturn are in the ascendant, Jupiter is in the fifth house, and the Sun is in the tenth house, [the same result follows].
If Venus and Mercury are situated in the eleventh house or the tenth house, the victory of the querent is certain.
If Venus occupies the eighth house in that very yoga,
the enemy will have his power destroyed and will cut down the questioner from his very exertion.
Success is attained when Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon are situated in the ascendant, the sixth house, and the tenth house;
likewise, it is achieved when Jupiter, Venus, and the Sun are situated in the ascendant, the sixth house, and the eighth house.
The acquisition of ministers occurs when Saturn and Mars are in the first house;
victory is attained when Mercury is in the fourth, the Moon is in the eighth, and Venus is in the seventh house.
When Saturn is in the tenth house, Jupiter is in the seventh, Venus is in the third,
and the Moon is in the sixth, while the remaining planets occupy the ascendant, the querent's victory is certain.
In the Sahaja yoga, victory occurs when the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are present along with benefics situated in the ascendant;
or when Jupiter is in the ascendant while malefics are stationed in the eleventh or the tenth house.
When Jupiter and the Moon are in the sixth house from the ascendant, there is victory at the end; when Venus and the Moon are there, there is victory in the undertaking if the Sun is in a sharp sign.
Thus, the auspicious yogas based on victory have been declared for the time of questioning;
however, the inauspicious ones also occur therein, which I shall explain hereafter.
In battle, defeat occurs when the ninth house and the ascendant are occupied by Saturn, the Moon, and Yama (Mars).
Death occurs when the Moon and Yama are in the ascendant and are aspected by Mars and Saturn.
If Saturn is in the eighth house in a retrograde motion and the Sun is in the ascendant, death occurs;
or if the Moon is situated in the third, eleventh, or eighth house along with the Sun, one should predict execution.
If Venus, Mercury, and the Moon are in the seventh house, there is destruction for the querent even while traveling;
furthermore, if Mars and Venus are in the ascendant, there is an increase in hunger, disease, and enemies.
If the Moon and Mars are in the sixth house, Mercury and Venus are in the ascendant,
and the Sun is situated in the eighth house, the death of the minister is to be known.
The death of the son of the querent occurs when malefic planets occupy the ascendant or the fifth house;
likewise, there is failure if Mars is with the Moon in the ascendant and aspected by Saturn.
When the Moon is situated in the seventh or the eighth house and the Sun has entered the ascendant—
or in the reverse case— the traveler will encounter fear, defeat, or death.
When malefic planets are situated in the second, third, or trine houses, and the benefics are devoid of strength,
while the Moon is located in the eighth house, the querent faces imprisonment, death, or ruin.
If Mars and the Moon are in the seventh house, there is a conflict between them when the Sun and Mercury rise;
likewise, in a battle between Saturn and Mars, there is defeat, and the same applies to Mercury and the Sun.
In the ninth [house], however, when all [planets] are present, the king destroys his ministers and domestic priests;
in this yoga, if the Moon is rising, he destroys his son, chief architect, and preceptor.
If the Sun and Saturn are in the ascendant and aspected by Mars,
and the Moon is in the seventh house while the benefics are weak, there is the death of the querent's army commander.
When the Moon is in its sign of debilitation or retrogression, the Sun is in the seventh house,
and Mercury is in the third house, the king, having exerted his prowess, is slain along with his minister.
If the ascendant (lagna) is at its rising in the head (mūrdhodaya), or is joined with or aspected by benefics and friends,
and if the benefics are strong in the ascendant belonging to a benefic division (varga),
it bestows success; otherwise, it is not desired.
Another [method] is undertaken through the logic of birth, departure, and results.
If malefic planets are situated in the eighth, fourth, twelfth, seventh,
or second houses from the Lagna or the Moon, they do not produce auspicious results for the men who inquire; however, when these same positions are occupied by benefics, they are highly praised.
At the time of departure, one should contemplate this entire world as both existent and non-existent.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Vijayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā— these [lunar days] produce results in this manner.
In the bright fortnight, the lunar days (tithis) are to be considered as inferior, middling, and excellent respectively; in the dark fortnight, they are the reverse.
All lunar days (tithis) in the bright fortnight are recommended, while in the dark fortnight, some authorities exclude the thirtieth day.
Furthermore, even if one sets out on the sixth or eighth day when the Vasu asterism is attained, that journey quickly meets with destruction, as does setting out on the twelfth day.

Some declare that the result occurs on the first day (pratipad) and not on the fifteenth; this [view] has been rejected by those who know the subject, and thus it must be considered as merely dismissible.
Surely they said this after having observed something or other; when there is a contradiction between equally authoritative statements, by whom can propriety be determined?
Chapter 4: The Strength of the Lunar Mansions (Nakṣatra-bala)

In every direction, the seven classes beginning with the Bahulas have already set out; situated in the wind and fire quarters, he who wields an exceedingly fierce rod moves transversely. Even the Lord of the Gods undergoes great hardship when attempting to cross him.
But surely there would be a contradiction if the quarters were each occupied by only a single staff?
The remaining [gates], excluding the one facing south from the eastern gate, do not conflict with the rule of circumambulation; thus the intermediate directions (vidiś) should be determined.
A king may, at his pleasure, even cross over the staff-mark (daṇḍa), provided he avoids the trident-mark (śūla) and maintains purity regarding the orientation of the cardinal points.
In Jyeṣṭhā, Bali, having gone toward the direction of Indra (the east), met with bondage;
in Ājapada, Mura, having gone toward the south (the direction of Yama), fell under the power of Murāri;
and in Rohiṇī, Namuci, having gone toward the west (the direction of Varuṇa), met his destruction by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having gone toward the quarter presided over by Soma and Aryaman, Śambara fell under the power of death.
Puṣya, Hasta, Śravaṇa, and Śraviṣṭhā are said to face the east and other directions; Aśvinī and Uttarāṣāḍhā face north.
Furthermore, some say that Rohiṇī, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Revatī are the intermediate [directions].
Those known as Sarvadvārika, Guru, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Anurādhā;
those of Indra, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, and the Vasus—these eight, together with the first [Aśvinī], are always excellent.
That which is associated with Raudra, Ārdrā, Ahi, Bhaga, Svāti, Anila, Anala, Maghā, Śakra, and Agni is censured.
The vehicle [is located] between Tvaṣṭṛ and Anila, and between Agni and Yama, as well as between Pitṛ and Ara.

All [asterisms], even those considered pure by sages, are honored for their respective activities; however, for one desiring to conquer the enemy, an expedition at sunrise when the sun is in Leo (Anale) is auspicious. Victory attends the traveler under Rohiṇī, the three Uttaras, and Viśākhā.
Having abandoned the first part of the day, Garga spoke to those seeking supreme sovereignty.

One should set out for the destruction of enemies during the first half of the day when the moon is in Mūla, Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Uraga (Āśleṣā), or Śaṅkara (Ārdrā), excluding the latter half of the day.

One may set out for the sake of one's servants during the second half of the day when the moon is in Pavana (Svātī), Aśvin (Aśvinī), Sūrya (Hasta), or Guru (Puṣya), excluding the first half of the day.
However, one desiring splendor should not set out at the beginning of the night when the moon is in Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Maitra (Anurādhā), Śaśi (Mṛgaśiras), or Tvāṣṭra (Citrā).
Excluding the middle watch of the night, one should avoid the first part of the night for the constellations Bharaṇī and those belonging to the Pitṛs (Maghā) when intending to kill.
One who seeks wealth should travel during the three periods beginning with Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇā) at the end of the night, but not under Punarvasu.
Some prohibit the period known as Ambupa (Pūrvaphalgunī), including its portion at the end of the night, during midday.
Arriving at any desired time is praised when the moon is in the asterisms of Hasta, Indravaiśvadeva, Upendra, or Surejya;
having set out on a journey under Śravaṇa, a king seeking prosperity should never enter his own capital.
Having gone to and stayed in the Saumya [asterism], and having set out from the Raudra or Āditya [asterisms], the king overcomes hosts of enemies.
Having gone to the Maitra [asterism] and stayed in the Pūrvaphalgunī [asterism],
the king should march from the Mūla [asterism] for the destruction of his foes.
Having gone to Hastā and stayed through the night in Svātī or Citrā, one who sets out under Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā) or Agni (Kṛttikā) overcomes his enemies.
Or, having stayed for one night at the boundary under Tiṣya (Puṣya), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), or Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), the traveler attains prosperity.
If the lunar mansion is conjoined with malefic planets, there is internal strife and loss of fortune; if it is afflicted by Rāhu or the Sun, there is disease.
If it is afflicted by Ketu or a meteor, there is destruction of the country and suffering, as is the case when Saturn or Mars is present.
Furthermore, when a planet is surrounded by smoke, trembles, or is joined with dust, there will be affliction from misfortune, disease, exhaustion, and illness.
When a planet is split by another, it falls under the power of the enemy; and when struck by lightning during twilight or night, it is said that there will be a failure of horses.
Having observed birth and so forth, as well as action, the non-existent,
the composite, and the portion of the stars, one should give the tenth.
And the twenty-third is named the Destruction of Delusion.

From the first [nakṣatra], the twenty-fifth is this mental one; a man [born] under six such asterisms would be a king. A king born under a human asterism (Mānava-nakṣatra) has that very same asterism as his consecration asterism.
The results of these [planets], whether good or bad, correspond to their names through their desired qualities or sinful defects;
when there is purity regarding the birth asterism and so forth, one who has set out conquers enemies before long.
Those [planets] arisen from the birth, lord of the year, and lord of the day cause prosperity,
adversity, security, the enemy, the achiever, the destroyer, the friend, and the over-friend respectively.
Just as one attains the success of friends, enemies, and neutral parties during auspicious actions,
so too does one who has gone before the consecration attain it, and not in any other circumstances.

Having bathed under the Puṣya asterism with water containing white mustard, śāli rice, priyaṅgu, and madayantī, one should proceed toward the east; or, under the Saumya asterism, with water containing a thousand māṇika measures.
Having bathed with water under the asterism Hasta, the king should set out toward the southern direction.
In the month of Caitra, having bathed in rivers crowded with sages, one should travel toward the eastern direction;
but in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should travel toward the western direction using the mud and waters of river confluences.
Having bathed with waters mixed with *madhuka*, *bhadradāru*, and *dāru* during the *udak-śraviṣṭhās*,
one should [offer] vessels made from the horns of cows and elephants, filled with honey and ghee, during the *pauṣṇa* [nakṣatra].
Having bathed in the north during the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice with honey, *pūthikā*, and the waters of a completed work of merit (*pūrta*),
and having offered oblations into the fire with the mantras of the lunar mansions and the gods, one obtains victory.
Unbroken *māṣa* beans, boiled rice mixed with sesame, and cow’s curd;
and the meat of a bull and of a deer [are the offerings] for the five [deities] beginning with Āśvina.
The food for Śaṅkara and the others consists of blood, melted fat, milk-rice, and the flesh of serpents;
for the ancestors, it is rice mixed with sesame and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, following the two lunar mansions.
One may eat priyaṅgu, variegated eggs, fruits, barley-gruel, and kulattha beans;
likewise, honey and ghee from the hand, as well as roots, water, and flour-meal, starting from the root [of the list].
On the day of Śravaṇā and the other [nakṣatras], one should eat śāli rice,
vegetables, cat meat, ghee, meat as desired, and barley meal mixed with black gram.
Having consumed clarified butter, sesame-rice, fish, and milk in clockwise order,
the king should eat according to the direction assigned by the lunar mansion for the sake of success.
Food that is tasteless, infested with fallen hair and flies, foul-smelling, causing decay, or insufficient, as well as that which is burnt, is unfavorable.
However, food that is well-cooked, soft, beautiful, agreeable to the mind, delicious, and abundant leads to victory at the time of marching.
Traveling by day is beneficial when the lunar day (*tithi*) is auspicious and the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) is unfavorable;
traveling by night is recommended when the asterism is favorable and the lunar day is devoid of good qualities.
Therefore, one who travels against the direction of the wind incurs the defects described for both the asterisms and the lunar days.
The sage Bhṛgu also correctly declared the merits for those two who have set out on their journey.
On the day of the Sun (Sunday), one experiences diseases of the stomach and eyes, afflictions from wild beasts and forest-dwellers, and even the loss of wealth.
On the day of the Moon, one who possesses strength will suffer from diseases arising from wind, phlegm, and fever, loss of food, and afflictions produced by water.

During the day of the Son of the Sun (Saturn), one who travels suffers from fever, wounds, poison, blood disorders, bilious ailments, pain, and oppression by enemies; he is harassed by hosts of foes, meets with wretchedness, and undergoes separation from kinsmen and wealth, as well as death, imprisonment, and disease.
When Mercury is situated on a Saturday, one afflicts enemies through the power of mantras, attains pleasant stories and the acquisition of arts and friends,
and very soon secures for oneself, during the day of the Sun, land, wealth, victory, jewels, women, majesty, and joy.
On a Saturday, one enjoys excellent young women, beds, garments, perfumes, food, drink, remembrance of past pleasures, wealth, and jewels during the day;

however, if the Sun is in a state of non-increase (*anupacaya*), even a favorable day is unfavorable, whereas if it is situated in a state of increase (*upacaya*), even that which is designated as evil brings about auspicious results.
Chapter 6: Muhūrta (Auspicious Moments)
The lunar mansions (karaṇas) excluding Gara, Viṣṭi, and Parigha are desired for a traveler.
Some authorities also recommend Gara, while Vaṇija is recommended specifically for mercantile activities.
Furthermore, the asterisms born of Indra, Agni, Indra, Niśācara, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Yama are auspicious during the day.
Rudra, Āhirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Dasras, Antaka, Agni, Dhātṛ,
Indra, Aditi, Guru, Hari, Arka, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Anila— these are the names of the moments (kṣaṇas) during the night.
A fifteenth part of the day and likewise of the night is designated by the term *muhūrta*.
And that [time] should be known by those who know it through skillful means, using shadows, water-clocks, and water.
Like the constellations, the *parigha* and other [omens] occurring at moments should be considered together with their presiding deities;
that very same result has been observed by Garga and others, and there are verses regarding this: [The verses follow.]
A full day and night is conjoined with the moon and the lunar mansions;
those lunar mansions and muhūrtas are traditionally held to possess qualities corresponding to their respective actions.
In the eighth half-day of an even [fortnight], there is an auspicious moment known as Viriñca-vibhu;
by means of that, departing toward the south, victory in all directions is praised.
(Chapter 7: Lunar Strength)
Satya said: "The Moon, who removes the conceptualizations of the movements of rebirth, desires to go to the birth [of Śiva];
however, he is born there in a new body, and for that reason, he is not considered an adept in ritual acts."
And since that very ascendant (lagna), which is the body itself, has been purified by him through many [means],
what auspicious thing could he not declare as bringing prosperity to those who possess bodies equal to his own?

When the Moon, purified by the *aṣṭavarga* system, attains its state of excellence, then even if it is situated in the house of birth, it is praised; for that which bestows auspiciousness through the *aṣṭavarga* is truly beautiful.

A planet situated in the seventh, fifth, tenth, sixth, third, or first house from the Moon is not auspicious; however, it becomes beneficial if it is placed in the second, eighth, or eleventh house, or if it occupies the opposite houses from those mentioned.

For one for whom there is a measure of the fruit of the objective field (*gocara*), is the fruit of penetration (*vedha*) desired or not? Generally, this is not widely accepted, for the objective field yields the fruit of the coarse path.
If the moon passes to the left (apasavya) of a person’s natal asterism, that ruler of the earth encounters calamity.
Likewise, when Venus and the other planets enter the houses of others, there is victory for one over the other; however, during the dark fortnight, there is loss.

If the lord of the zodiac sign occupied by the Moon at birth is in a house of increase (upacaya) or in the ascendant at the time of departure, there is loss for the traveler; however, if that lord of the lunar mansions is in a waning phase, there is gain.

At the beginning of the fortnight, if the lord is in a house of decrease, there is loss; but if it is in a waxing phase, gain is declared. However, when the moon is in its waning state, situated at the start of the dark fortnight, [the result] diminishes.
If the Moon is joined with a house of increase, moving to the left (waxing) during the bright fortnight while desiring auspiciousness, or is situated between benefics;
or if the Moon is joined with a friendly or submissive house even in a *kāraka*-constellation, it bestows the fruits of victory and happiness; otherwise, it is their destroyer.
If the lord of the sign occupied by the Moon is in a state of waning or even in a neutral position, one may set out with confidence provided he is in the *vaśya* or *karkaṣa* state of friendship.
If this is not the case, one should not travel even if the Moon is full or in a house of gain, whether from the house of its rising or its own natal house.
When the Moon is eclipsed by Venus or Mercury, there is death; when eclipsed by Mars or Saturn, there is fear; and when eclipsed by Ketu, there is the loss of one's wife.
When the Moon’s rays are dimmed in beauty, there is an increase in enemies; and when it is surrounded by a distorted halo, there is blindness.
Chapter 8: The Strength of the Ascendant (Lagnabala)
All bipeds are subject to the lion, as are all quadrupeds with the exception of the lion; and the species of aquatic creatures and reptiles are subject to the bear.
These remain under the control of the lord of beasts, excluding the reptiles. What has been stated regarding houses should be understood according to common worldly practice.
Terrestrial creatures, aquatic beings, and reptiles submit to the power of their own kind after observing its strength.
Likewise, those who are even-tempered by day become subject to the influence of uneven planets at night, while those who are uneven by day become subject to the influence of even planets at night.
When the [ascendant] rises at the head, there is the accomplishment of desired undertakings; when it rises at the back, there is fruitlessness and the flight of one's forces.
For one who has set out toward the direction of the destination, success comes easily; however, if the [ascendant] is in a retrograde direction, one’s exertion becomes futile.

Travel during the day is recommended when the planets possess daytime strength, and at night when they possess nocturnal power; travel is not recommended when the planets possess the opposite strength in their respective signs.
When the Moon, the Sun, and the Ascendant are conjoined with planets that are in their signs of exaltation, mūlatrikoṇa, own sign, or both, the journey bestows an increase of land and prosperity.
When Pisces is on the ascendant for one departing on a journey, the path becomes crooked, fraught with obstacles, and there is a failure to return after completing one's task.
This same result occurs even when other signs are present, provided Pisces is included, or when the signs of Pisces are situated within the asterisms of another sign.
"When [Saturn] is in the eighth house from the enemy, there is the destruction of the enemy; when it is in the sixth house and situated in the ascendant, there is the death of the traveler.
This is the instruction of Satya in the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā], yet this is not an absolute rule."
If, at the time of the enemy's birth, the eighth house is joined by malefic planets,
or if the sixth house is joined by benefic planets, then from those two [houses] there will be good and evil results respectively.
When Venus is in its own sign (svalagna) conjoined with the ascendant, one attains results without affliction, the destruction of enemies, and the fulfillment of goals while traveling abroad.
Some say that when it is in the second house, there is loss of wealth, exhaustion, and misfortune; however, others say there is the arrival of auspiciousness, happiness, and prosperity.
In the third [house], there is gain from servants, wealth, vehicles, companions, and victory; in the fourth, there is imprisonment, loss of wealth, fear, and the destruction of the army.

In the fifth house, there is the failure of counsel, internal dissension, calamity, and danger to one's sons; in the sixth, there is the increase of enemies, yet also the acquisition of enemy wealth, power, splendor, and victory.

In the seventh house (the dyūna), there is misfortune regarding travel and vehicles, hunger, excessive exhaustion, affliction, imprisonment, death, humiliation, and diseases. In the eighth house (the nidhana), there is loss of wealth, illness, failure in undertakings, fear, and danger from force even without any specific task, as well as decay. In the ninth house (the dharma), there is loss of wealth, disease, failure in duties, and fears; in the tenth house (the kārya), there is danger from force and depletion.
Some say that this [result] is supported by accumulation; therefore, from that, there is auspicious movement when the [planet] goes to the tenth house.

There is the attainment of wealth, brilliance, the accomplishment of auspicious goals, and victory in the eleventh house (lābha); in the eighth (riphpha), there is deceit; and in the twelfth (vyaya) or the fourth (bhaya), even if one is victorious, there is division.

If a malefic planet rises in the house of birth, there is death of a son and lack of success; if it is in the fifth house from that, one suffers distress in gambling and later attains happiness from the house of birth. If it is in the ninth house, there is a turning back from the path; if in the tenth house (Meṣūraṇa), there is the acquisition of wealth.
Just as it is with the remaining signs from the ascendant, so too is the result from the natal sign.
If the Sun is in the eastern ascendant (the first house), there is suffering from hunger and thirst, loss of the way, eye disease, and the acquisition of afflictions.
If the Moon is there, it is auspicious; if Mars is there, there is suffering for the sake of deities in one's own country, as well as affliction from bile disorders, snakes, weapons, and fire.

In the sub-period of Baudha (Mercury), there is satisfaction, the attainment of what is desired, and fame; in that of Jaiva (Jupiter), there is acquisition, status, honor, and the destruction of enemies; in that of Śaukra (Venus), there is the acquisition of a jewel-like woman and the success of one's undertakings; and in that of Mānda (Saturn), there is imprisonment, disease, and humiliation by those of low status.
Even a benefic planet that does not grant auspicious nourishment at birth should not occupy the ascendant for one who is traveling;
however, even a malefic planet that produces auspicious results for men, they declare its position in the ascendant to be desirable.
If the house of one's own birth sign or birth star is not subject to control for those traveling,
even a favorable ascendant will result in the loss of wealth and great exhaustion.
When the natal ascendant and the natal star have come under the influence of a friend,
even if the current ascendant and star cause a loss of strength, the traveler will swiftly obtain victory, wealth, and honor.
Some say that the house in which a planet makes a *niraṃśa* [conjunction] is the ascendant;
it is unfavorable for one who departs, because it bestows fear, grief, and agitation.

The sages declare that travel is inauspicious even when the ascendant is occupied by Taurus, Scorpio, or Cancer, provided they are favorable to the person; it is likewise inauspicious even when these signs occupy other asterisms.
When Venus enters the ascendant, it brings about the attainment of results for one desiring to travel even without effort;
a journey by boat is auspicious when the sign of water is the ascendant, and likewise when its degree rises, even if another sign is the ascendant.
Chapter 9: Varieties of the Ascendant.
The *horā* may be upright, horizontal, or bent; it is released, traversed, or not yet reached by the sun in due order.
These [terms] are found in the instruction of Jīvaśarman; the zodiac sign (*rāśi*) is to be understood according to the system of Brahmaṣaṇḍa.
Some say that the *horā* should be the one that rises above the first six signs in each successive mandala;
however, Vasiṣṭha declares the *horā* to be determined by the *drekkāṇas* as they successively arrive at the ascendant for each sign.
All is authoritative because it was taught by the Sage; however, in this matter, only the *dala* (digit) is to be applied as the *horā*.
One should count the others starting from that half in which the thousand-rayed sun is situated, with its face turned sideways.

If the crow goes with its face upward while perched on the *lagna*, it accomplishes the desired task without hardship; if it goes with its face turned sideways, it brings about the exhaustion of toil and suffering;
if it goes with its face downward, it causes the rout of the army and the arrival home only with great difficulty.
All [planets] bestow nourishment and fruit when seen by their own lord and not by malefic planets.

Whatever results are produced by the planets and the day, the *horā* of the traveler produces all of that for him. Except for the effects of cold water and rain, there is nothing that the lunar *horā* does not bring about, including the acquisition of jewels through association with young women.
One should apply results corresponding to the form, activity, and qualities of the *drekkāṇa* for the sake of determining victory:
if the *drekkāṇa* is gentle in appearance, endowed with flowers and fruit, or possessed of jewels and vessels;
if it is aspected by benefics, there will be victory; and if it is joined with weapons and aspected by malefics, there will be defeat.
In that case, there is burning in fire, or imprisonment with a serpent around the neck, and the traveler is bound with a noose.
If the Drekkāṇa of Jupiter occupies the ascendant, there is gain from the king; if it is in the second house, gain from ministers;
if in the third house, gain from physicians, priests, and astrologers; and if in other houses, gain from servants.
Consideration of the location and valor, valor in activity, the strength of the army,
food and drink, and bedding and seating— these are the five [factors] in their respective order.
In the tenth [period], there are vehicles, seats, beds, and carriages; others [in the same period] include food and drink.
In the thirteenth [period], there are mounts and warriors, and thereafter comes the crown prince.
The strength of the traveler, the knowledge of the mantra, and its determination depend upon that [the Sun];
enemies are found in the four decans (drekkāṇas) beginning with the fifteenth degree of Libra.
In the nineteenth [year], there are soldiers and wealth on a bed of water; thereafter come riches, and after that, a commander of the army, followed by disturbances to the military.
Therefore, one should place the commander of the army at the twenty-fourth [digit] to protect the vulnerabilities of the host;
the health of the troops and the four-footed animals should be protected in the subsequent triad.
In the first three [houses], there is work, treasury, and the attainment of results; in the next three, there is sovereignty over the earth;
then follow the performance of dharma, the honoring of warriors, and the completion of a journey.
Thus, regarding the states such as rising and so forth which have been declared by me according to the decans (drekkāṇas),
their good and bad results are to be predicted from their conjunctions and aspects with those that are good or bad.
When the ninth part of the Sun is reached by the Ascendant, there is destruction of its vehicle;
when it is in the portion of the Moon, there is a return to one's own home with difficulty and a softening of its brilliance.
In the portion of Mars, there is fear of fire; in that of Mercury, the acquisition of friends and the arrival of wealth;
in that of Jupiter, an increase in enjoyments; and in the portion of Venus, the son of the Sun (Saturn), the destruction of servants.

Whatever fruit is prescribed for a planet at its rising, its ninth-part (navāṃśaka) produces that same result when it is in the ascendant. Here, if the ninth-part is in a benefic house, the traveler receives assistance; if it is in an enemy's strength-portion, he encounters opposition.

Whatever result was declared for the rising of a sign (rāśi) should also be stated for the rising of its twelfth part (dvādaśāṃśa); and whatever is ordained for the ninth-part (navāṃśa), that shall apply to the rising of the thirtieth-part (triṃśāṃśa). Chapter 10: The Strength of Planetary Positions (Graha-sthāna-bala)
In its rising, the Sun causes fever, grief, disease, and obstacles; in the second month, it destroys prosperity, honor, strength, and the heart;
in the third, it bestows gold, food, coral, jewels, and land; and in the fourth, it brings about detachment, strife with kinsmen, and the destruction of pleasure.
In the fifth house, the Sun causes trouble regarding sons; on the road, he brings success in one's aims; in the sixth house, the attainment of desired fruits and the destruction of enemies;
in the seventh house, quarrels with the wife and the depletion of wealth; and in the eighth house, he causes death and disease.
In the ninth [year], he destroys the Dharma; in the tenth, having lost his wealth, he commits violence in the air while his labor and work remain unrecognized.
Having acquired great wealth from the arrival of jewels, he incurs expenditure; and having spent it, he ends up with only a small amount of profit.
If the Moon is in the ascendant, it causes quarrels and sorrow when not full; however, if full, it bestows women, horses, jewels, friends, and sons.

In the second house, it grants young women, jewels, and wealth. In the third house, it provides brothers and gains from friends. But in the fourth house, if it is waning, it brings about their destruction.

When the Moon is in the fifth house, it bestows wealth but causes grief for one's children; it creates enmity with friends and brings no happiness in the sixth house. In the seventh house, it grants wealth and women but destroys wealth; in the eighth house, the subtle Moon causes death and grief for the traveler.
In the ninth house, it returns quickly and accomplishes its purpose; when waned, there is loss, and when in the sky (the tenth), there is growth, being otherwise in other positions.
In the eleventh house, one attains sovereignty, happiness, and the gain of wealth; when situated in the twelfth, there are afflictions, loss, expenditure, and fears.
If Mars is in the ascendant, there will be affliction from poison, fire, blood, weapons, and blows; if situated in the second house, he destroys one's strength but later bestows wealth.

Occupying the third house, Mars brings the acquisition of young women, jewels, wealth, and garments, yet causes the loss of kinsmen and fear of enemies; in the fourth house, he grants these gains but also brings fear of enemies.
Mars, situated in the fifth house, brings about the purification of one's station; as an enemy [in the sixth], he quickly effects the destruction of foes.
Occupying the seventh house, he causes loss of wealth, lack of pleasure, and affliction by disease; in the eighth house, he brings about imprisonment, loss of wealth, illness, and fear of death.
When Mars enters the ninth house (Dharma), it does not accomplish dharma; it is declared inauspicious in the tenth house (Ambaram) and not a bestower of good fortune.

In the eleventh house (Lābha), it grants the attainment of wealth, success, and prosperity for one who sets out on a journey; however, when it has gone to the twelfth house (Riṣpha), it causes great loss of wealth.

In the ascendant, one obtains fame, happiness, wealth, intelligence, and victory; in the second house, wealth; in the third, one becomes longing and detached; in the fourth, one attains all desires; in the fifth, the splendor of beds, food, and drink, as well as the arrival of sons.
In the sixth house, if Mercury is present, there is oppression by enemies and the traveler will experience distress.
If Mercury is in the seventh house from the Sun or Jupiter, there is the acquisition of an excellent wife, clothing, and wealth;
some say there is suffering, while others declare it to be auspicious when it is in the eighth house.
If it is in the ninth house, there is an increase in merit, and if it is in the tenth house, one's desired success shall be attained.
In the eighth house (Riṣpha), one should predict the effortless acquisition of knowledge from others and expenditure.
If Jupiter is in the ascendant, there is fame; in the second house, the attainment of wealth; in the third house, hunger, fatigue, and affliction;
in the fourth house (the netherworld), pride in the principles of dharma; and even when situated in the fifth house, one's undertakings succeed, though they may otherwise be difficult to accomplish.

If Jupiter is in the sixth house, an enemy approaches; some say he comes under one's control, while others say one falls under the enemy's control. In this position, one incurs misfortune, women, and infamy; yet others have declared that when it is in the eighth house (Mṛtyu), it destroys life.
When Jupiter is in the tenth house, there is the birth of a son, the accomplishment of dharma, and the attainment of wealth and fame through one's actions.
When it is in the eleventh house, desired undertakings reach fulfillment; when it reaches the twelfth house, one suffers from manifold miseries.
If Venus is in the ascendant, there is the attainment of pleasure through courtesans, wealth, clothing, garlands, and food; in the second house, there is gain;

and one who has traveled does not suffer but attains excellent learning. In the seventh house, there is the arrival of friends; in the fifth house, there is the acquisition of position, wealth, and honor.
In the sixth house, they say there is the defeat of enemies, lack of pleasure, and grief; otherwise, it is said to be in its proper place.
When Venus (Bhārgava) is in the seventh house, having given away the woman’s wealth, it causes the destruction of one's own territory;

however, when in the eighth or ninth house, it accomplishes the task and quickly fulfills the desire. When in the tenth house, it bestows abundant wealth upon the traveler, and in the eleventh house, it grants victory and wealth.
If [the lord] goes to the twelfth house, he makes expenditure useless; however, he is praised by others when situated in the twelfth.
If Saturn is in the ascendant, one suffers imprisonment and death; if in the second house, one experiences loss of wealth as well as some auspicious gain.
If situated in the third house, he destroys the strength of his enemies; if in the fourth house, he faces danger from kinsmen and others.
If Saturn is in the fifth house, there is no accomplishment of one's goals; if situated in the sixth house, he brings about enemies without effort.
When in the seventh house, there is a loss of enthusiasm and eye diseases; when in the eighth house, death occurs through poison, fire, weapons, and the like, involving one's wife.
When Saturn is situated in the tenth house, one does not obtain merit through religious duty, nor happiness, nor a vehicle, nor the fruits of one's actions, even when healthy;
however, if it is in the eleventh house, there is gain of victory and wealth, whereas if it is in the twelfth house, the traveler gains no profit.

Generally, malefic planets situated in the periods (daśā) of their natural enemies do not [yield good results], whereas benefic planets— excluding those located in the sky (the tenth house) from the Sun— produce auspicious fruits everywhere; likewise, benefics produce auspicious results throughout.
Having abandoned the preceptor of the enemies of the gods who was situated in the eighth house, for one desiring victory.
Some say that Bhṛgu (Venus), having abandoned the sixth, twelfth, eighth, and third houses, is excellent;

the son of the Moon (Mercury) is excellent when situated in the twelfth, ninth, third, and seventh houses, but not otherwise. The Moon is honored when situated in the eleventh, fifth, second, ninth, third, and tenth houses.
The soul is said by Maṇittha to be omnipresent; it is not desired [to be] dependent on the last six signs or women.
Even according to the view of some, Bhṛgu (Venus) is auspicious, with the exception of the last house, the self, and gains;

the Moon is [auspicious] when situated in the third, sixth, eleventh, tenth, or eighth houses; and Budha (Mercury) is [auspicious] when situated in the seventh, the ascendant, the fifth, the fourth, the eleventh, or the twelfth house.
Chapter 11: General Rules and Exceptions.
That result which has been declared for planets situated in the ascendant and other houses, whether they be gentle or ungentle,
is not certain because of the variation in results when they have moved to positions corresponding to that same time.

Those who know the *horā* have declared this: when a planet is weak, even if it is the lord of the period (*daśā*) or the lord of the ascendant, it yields inauspicious results; and even if it is a benefic at its rising, it does not produce desirable results.

Now, a planet that is auspicious at birth, endowed with strength, and the lord of the period or a friend [of the lord], will yield auspicious results even if it is malefic; this is the verse proclaimed here by the Teacher.

Even a benefic planet is not to be employed [as a significator] if its results will occur only after a very long time; nor is a malefic planet to be used if its results are not yet imminent or if it has been conquered by an enemy. Furthermore, the lord of the *pāka* (the period) must be pure according to the *aṣṭakavarga* of its own domicile.
Likewise, the rule for the portions of the day [occupied by] the planets would be deficient and fruitless.

Some teachers maintain that the lord of the period (daśādhipa) should be gentle and situated in the ascendant (lagna), while the malefics should be in the upacaya houses and not in the ascendant; regarding this, there are two verses: [Verse 1] "The lord of the year, the lord of the month, and the lord of the day—these three lords should be gentle, occupying the ascendant, the third house, the fifth house, the ninth house, or the eleventh house. [Verse 2] "If the lord of the year is in the ascendant, the lord of the month is in the seventh, and the lord of the day is in the sixth, it is called the 'Sarpa-yoga' (serpent configuration); in that case, death occurs within six months."

When the ascendant is occupied by gentle planets, the result is exclusively and certainly auspicious; when the rising sign is occupied by malefic planets, there is no doubt that it is inauspicious for one who sets out.

Therefore, one should place a cruel planet that is the lord of its own period (daśā) and endowed with the quality of strength in the houses of increase; by no means should it be placed in the ascendant.
And since that [karma] is contradictory for them, how could it yield its own fruit in other states?
Thus, the destruction of the fruit occurs for everyone who desires the fruit.
Therefore, this [method] is not absolute; one should not determine good or bad solely by observing the *jātaka*.
Maṇittha and Vasiṣṭha have stated that the *śloka*, the *vṛtta*, and the *bheda* [are the criteria].
Those who were protectors and craftsmen during one's birth,
even if they are sinful, one may employ them without hesitation in the planetary positions of the departure-lagna.
Whatever yogas yielding auspicious or inauspicious results have been described in the context of nativities (jātaka),
one should apply all of them even during journeys after having carefully considered them.
If Saturn is in its own house within the ascendant, Mars is in Aries in its own house,
the Moon is in Libra, Mercury is in Gemini, and the Sun is in Leo, one should know that the birth of a king has occurred.
At the time of birth, some planets are situated in the rising sign of the Moon or in signs of increase;
all of those, whether known as various [types of] malefics or equalized by benefics, must be considered.
Whichever planet is situated in the tenth house from another becomes subject to its control by necessity;
likewise, whichever planet is situated in a *paṇaphara* house becomes a protector for that [planet].
Those planets that have entered houses of accumulation (upacaya) are mutually equal in their fame;
furthermore, the karakas (functional significators) were previously explained in the chapter on miscellaneous matters (prakīrṇaka).

Whichever planet is an enemy to both the lord of the birth sign and the lord of the ascendant, even if it is a benefic, it causes the destruction of the body when situated in the ascendant; whereas even a malefic that is a friend to those two produces auspicious results.
Even if a planet is auspicious for both the lord of one's birth sign and the lord of the ascendant, if it lacks the designation of being a "doer" (kāraka),
it will cause the traveler great fear and manifold destruction when it enters the ascendant.
Even a malefic planet, when situated in the ascendant, bestows auspiciousness upon men; it is known as the "agent" (kāraka).
Therefore, those desiring to travel should diligently consider this very matter according to the method of determining agents.

Even a single planet, though situated in its own sign, if it has entered an adverse course (vakrī), brings about various kinds of destruction for men even when located in the four houses [of the triplicity], or even if the entire group of planets has risen in the ascendant for travelers.
If the Sun is in the fifth house from the ascendant, it bestows joy through one's own children, women, and jewels;
however, if it occupies any other house, it quickly causes slaughter, imprisonment, and distress.
The Moon, having attained its rising and occupying all positions for those who have set out on a journey,
brings about an increase of enemies, the destruction of splendor, and obstacles.
In its own place, Mars situated in the ascendant bestows the destruction of enemies and victory;
however, when Mars has gone to any other house, it causes the loss of jewels and wealth.
When Mercury is situated in the houses of the Sun, Moon, or Mars, it brings about misfortune;
however, when it is in the ascendant, it bestows consecration, victory, wealth, and splendor for those associated with Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Jupiter, when situated in the place of Venus or the Moon, is declared to be a destroyer of wealth for the native;
in the remaining positions, however, it bestows land, friends, wealth, and victory.
In its own friendly place, Venus causes a loss of strength, yet bestows wealth and destroys enemies;
in the remaining places, it causes wind-fever and provokes enemies.
Saturn situated in the tenth house but placed in the ascendant brings about affection, happiness, and gain;
however, when situated in any other house, it is not auspicious, as it causes the destruction of prowess, strength, and honor.

The son of Savitṛ (Saturn), situated in its own sign, causes the destruction of wealth and limbs; the moon (the one with cold rays) brings the acquisition of excellent women; the sun brings sovereignty;
the son of the Earth (Mars) brings agitation to the army; and Mercury brings the hearing of pleasant news.
Then Jupiter brings the attainment of enjoyments, and Venus brings victory.
A planet situated on the southern path of the thousand-rayed sun, whether setting or rising,
causes the destruction of warriors, wealth, and the body of one who sets out on a journey at that very moment.
If a planet appears to the north of the sun, or sets [in conjunction] with it,
or occupies the midpoint of its orb at the time of the ascendant, it bestows flowers, garments, and food upon the traveler.
The alteration of its fixed course, luster, color, and magnitude is called *vikṛti* (transformation).
One situated in *vikṛti* or in its setting (*galana*) is not auspicious; however, one situated in its own house bestows auspiciousness.
One born under the asterism of Yāmya (Bharaṇī) is characterized by darkness; one born under Śravaṇa is Mercury; one born under Viśākhā is the Sun; and one born under Puṣya is Venus.
One born under Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Ābhāgya (Maghā), Ahi (Āśleṣā), or Kṛttikā is Saturn, Mars, Jupiter, or the Moon, respectively.
If a lunar mansion is struck by threefold portents and afflicted by powerful planets,
it must be avoided during a journey even if it is otherwise favorable when situated in the ascendant.
If the lord of the ninth house, an exalted planet, or a friend is in the ascendant, or if one of these is in its own division,
even a universal monarch comes under the control of the traveler, bowing his head in submission.
When the lord of the sign occupied by the Moon, or its division (varga), is in the ascendant, a king marching forth—
with his brave men and horses struck down— comes under the subjection of the enemy.
The houses (bhāvas) beginning with the tenth (karma), the eleventh (āgama), and the twelfth (vyaya), as well as the ascendants (udayas) and so forth, have been thus described.
The fruit of the journey is found in the fourth house; in the seventh house, there are enemies and negligence.
One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for these houses based on their conjunction with benefic or malefic planets.
In the opinion of Ācārya Satya, the Moon is commended for journeys when it is devoid of strength;
others, however, have declared that the Moon is commended only when it possesses directional strength (*digvīrya*).

Whatever result—whether good or bad—is prescribed for a planet situated at its time of rising during the departure [of a traveler], that same result in its entirety applies when that planet is in its own division (*varga*) or situated in the ascendant (*lagna*) on the day of the journey. 11.38.
Chapter 12: Miscellaneous.
One encounters great calamity during a Vyatīpāta yoga, or else meets with death upon its departure;
the same is taught for when one enters a Vaidhṛti yoga, as well as for those that touch for three days.
One should not travel during the deficient night (avamarātra), for there is misfortune in that; nor during an intercalary month (adhimāsaka), for there is calamity.
When the junction of seasons, solstices, and equinoxes occurs, a king desiring victory should not set out on a journey.
The results arising from the portions of friend, neutral, or enemy belonging to both the lord of one's own asterism and the lord of the period are declared to be the friends, neutrals,
and enemies of the seeker of victory during their respective ripening.
An enemy who is empty and in an unfavorable position must necessarily be utterly destroyed by one seeking victory;
likewise, one who has descended from his position should be oppressed, while one who is ascending should be weakened.
A king should not enter into an alliance with one who is currently in a similar state;
rather, he should form an alliance with one whose current state is unfavorable but whose future prospects are favorable through the ripening of good fortune.

In the opposite case, war is better; likewise, when Aśvinī is in a period of inauspicious future results, one should remain seated [in peace]. When the enemy is situated far away during the ripening of auspicious future results, one should remain seated.
If the lord of the *daśā* is endowed with strength and possesses auspicious aspects, there will be an increase in prosperity and one shall become a king;
if the opposite occurs, one shall go abroad; and if it is a mixed *daśā*, there will be a state of duality.
During a period afflicted by emptiness, during the ripening of the lord of the birth-ascendant's enemy,
or when the lord of one's own period and the karaka are in their periods, one should seek refuge with a sovereign.
One should go toward the direction of the planet that causes gain when the lord of that direction is strong and positioned in a *kaṇṭaka* house;
however, one should not do so even in thought if the lord of the direction lacks directional strength or is situated on the forehead (the eighth house).

The two lords of the birth and the rising signs, when endowed with strength and situated in houses of increase or in the *kaṇṭaka* positions, bestow auspicious results; even if they are malefic, they are always declared to be equal to benefics.

The lords of one's own house, the lord of the natal ascendant, and the Sun when situated at the junctions (sandhyā) are not auspicious; however, excluding Venus and Saturn, those planets emerging from the Sun are middling.
If Saturn and Mars, the Sun and the Moon, or Venus and Mars are situated in mutual trines,
they shall utterly destroy whatever results have been predicted and subsequently lead one toward their own respective directions.

If a planet's day is that of an enemy, it does not bestow auspicious results even if it is a benefic situated in the ascendant. Conversely, even a malefic planet produces a desired friend when it is situated in the ascendant on its own day.
The lords of the year, month, day, and hour are like thorns; they are powerful when situated in their respective positions.
For a traveler, the planets yield double the fruits—whether auspicious or inauspicious—as one proceeds further and further from them.
When the Sun has entered Leo, Aries, or Taurus, a journey is most excellent; it is middling when the Sun is in the houses of Saturn, Mercury, or Venus.
If the Sun is in Cancer, Pisces, or Scorpio, the journey is very long; however, according to the opinion of Devala, the Sun behind one on the road is auspicious.

In the *Āḍhya* system, the periods (*daśā*) grant their full fruits when they are superior; in the *Aṣṭavarga-śuddhi* system, they are middling; and in the systems based on the current ascendant, lunar day, weekday, and *karana*, they yield diminished results.
A journey is of the highest fruit when the benefic planets are in their triplicities, exaltations, or signs of increase;
it is middling when they have gone to the houses of their own friends; and it is inferior when they are in their signs of debilitation or inimical signs.
The sixth expedition, which is both middling and excellent, is favored by those who know the rules of expeditions.
When Venus has entered the opposite sign from its own division of the zodiac, when the sun has set at twilight,
and when Mercury is also situated in retrograde motion, a man who travels abroad falls under the power of others.
When Mercury has gone in direct motion and Venus is likewise situated thus,

Chapter 13: Tremors of the Body (Dehaspandana) I shall now describe the throbbing of the right side; its opposite results from the left.
