through gentle ascendants, lunar days, and asterisms, there is auspiciousness, while otherwise, it becomes inauspicious.

If there is the breaking or chipping of the left or middle tooth due to the rubbing against the banks of a river by trees bearing milk, fruit, or flowers, it brings about the destruction of enemies; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
With a stumbling gait, his ears suddenly bristling, and appearing extremely dejected, he pants softly and very deeply while resting his hands upon the ground;
with eyes rapidly blinking, prone to sleep, contrary, and causing fear, he eats unwholesome things and repeatedly voids blood and excrement.
Crushing anthills, stumps, shrubs, bushes, and trees at will, with its gaze fixed upon whatever it sees,
it should proceed in the direction of the march with swift steps, holding its head high; and at the time of donning the armor,
it repeatedly emits spray or trumpets loudly.

Or at that time, the attainment of intoxication brings victory, as does the biting of the right jaw. This brief presentation of the signs and gestures of horses, according to the *Vājilakṣaṇa*, is for the sake of the victory of kings, since it conveys even a fraction of their turning movements.
Furthermore, inauspicious [marks] are found on the testicles, the navel, the hump, the anus, the left side of the belly, and the feet.
Those [hair-whorls] situated on the throat, ears, and temples; those located on the middle of the back, the eyes, and above them;
those on the lips, the brows, the thighs, the arms, the belly, and the sides—together with those on the forehead, they are most auspicious.
When there is an inquiry regarding the scattering of hair, neighing, smoke, flames, and so forth, these are the signs to be observed;
in this matter, the verses composed by Viṣṇugupta are proclaimed as authoritative for horses.
In that regard, by way of general rule, their flaming occurs when they rest on the western part of the seat;
it is not desired otherwise, nor is it auspicious when occurring on the left or right sides in that manner.

The same [results] apply to the feet, the tuft of hair, and the tail; however, sparks, burning, and smoke are specified for the back, the hindquarters, and the tail as being equal to the previously mentioned results.
If there is a blaze or smoke at the penis, it portends a disturbance within the inner apartments.

If there are constantly rays like those of a child, or if there are burns, flames, sparks, particles, and smoke upon the shoulders, the seat, and the shoulder-region, it portends death and captivity in battles.

When flames emerge from the chest, eyes, forehead, or forelegs of horses, or from the mouths of neighing horses, they grant victory; however, the emergence of smoke portends the destruction of the master.
During the nights when the nostrils, the flow of tears, the lips, the head,
and the eyes blaze with coppery, black, green, or variegated colors, there is a flaming omen for victory.
Indeed, for victory, the blazing of these two—when they are very white and of the color of a parrot—is always auspicious;
and thus, according to the circumstances, is the result even with other mounts.
Therefore, one should carefully observe the neighing that reveals what is desired or undesired;
and that which arises from a neck extended like a mountain peak yields a desirable result.
When horses look toward their right side, with mouths full of mouthfuls of fodder, uttering sounds that are loud, resonant, and deep,
and when they rejoice in their bits, food, drink, armor, their master, and their equipment,
it leads to the accomplishment of all goals.
During the twilights, when their neighing causes confusion as they face the blazing quarters of the sky, and when sleep has been deeply lost,
these horses produce fear and bring about slaughter, captivity, and defeat.
Those with tails curved [over their backs], lying on their right sides, are not desired;
those striking the surface of the earth with their left forefeet should be known as portending travel abroad.

Yawning, shaking the back, repeatedly pawing the ground with the hooves, scratching with the feet, and the appearance of horses as if preparing for a military expedition— these are the signs of one desiring to lick [the earth].
Horses that are drowsy, sluggish, and have dark eyes; whose thoughts are lost in deep reflection and whose memories are vacant during the day;
and who, at night, lose their sleep due to mutual agitation—such horses bring no good fortune to their master.

If one smears the shins—which are free of wounds and hair—and the feet, with clay while the body is thrilled, it leads to victory; however, if the opposite occurs regarding the two hind legs, one should exert effort to restrain oneself while facing the direction of the journey.
If a horse repeatedly voids urine and excrement, does not move in the direction of the whip even when struck,
is terrified of improper actions, and has tearful eyes, it does not bring welfare to its master.

When the king mounts, if a horse that follows the procession, endowed with discipline, neighs at another horse or touches its own right flank with its mouth, that horse will soon extend the royal fortune of its master. Chapter 23: Auspicious and Inauspicious Omens (Śakuna-śubhāśubha)
The auspicious or inauspicious karma performed by men in other previous births—
whatever ripening of that [karma] the *śakuna* (omen) announces to those who are traveling.
In cases of sounds, movements, glances, and utterances, males, females, and neuters are to be understood [respectively].

Because these belong to distinct classes and lack fixed stability, their specific manifestation cannot be discerned. These two verses were composed by the Sage regarding the description of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Those men whose limbs are plump, elevated, and well-proportioned, who have broad necks and chests,
whose cries are faint yet deep, and who possess steady prowess, are of firm valor.
Women whose necks, heads, and noses are slender, and whose mouths, feet, and gait are delicate, as well as those who speak with clarity and gentleness— women other than these are neuter (napuṃsaka).
One should observe from the world itself the conduct of village and forest dwellers and so forth;
desiring to examine them, I speak [of this] for the sole purpose of maintaining one's livelihood.

One should designate the king as the "pathyātman" (the one whose nature is beneficial) with respect to the army and the city, and the deity with respect to the caravan; however, in cases of equality, the one superior in birth, learning, or age should be designated.
In directions where the sun has set, risen, or is about to rise, the results are likewise;
those directions that are glowing with embers, smoky, or otherwise tranquil are of different [auspicious] kinds.
One should predict that the results for the five directions beginning with that [central one] are equal throughout the three periods of time;
as for the remaining two directions, the auspicious or inauspicious results should be stated according to their proximity.

The wise one should likewise declare the results: [an increase] quickly from those situated near or on low ground, and after a long time from those situated on high or distant ground; and he should state the results of the destruction or increase of the location accordingly.

A planet is "illuminated by fate" (daivadīpta) according to the sequence of moment, lunar day, asterism, wind, and sun; it is "illuminated by action" (kriyādīpta) through its movement, position, house, voice, and physical gestures.
Thus, although he is peaceful in ten ways, he is gentle when subsisting on grass and fruit;
he is fierce when consuming meat and impurities; and he is known as mixed when eating ordinary food.
They reside in palatial mansions, auspicious and delightful places,
and among the finest trees that bear sweet sap, fruit, and flowers.

At their own respective times, those moving on mountains and in water are strong; likewise, the night-walkers (nocturnal beings) are strong by day and night. Furthermore, eunuchs, women, and men are strong in ascending order [of their respective times].
Those endowed with strength by virtue of their speed, birth, power, position, joy, and essence are possessed of strength;
likewise, those that are in their own domain and in direct order are so endowed, while those that are the opposite of these are devoid of it.
The kaṃsakukkuṭa, ibha, cirilla, śikhin, vañjula,
chikkara, balina, siṃhanāda, and kūṭapūra [are the sounds] from the east.
And from the south come harsh sounds.
Cats, festivals, musical instruments, songs, and laughter are associated with Varuṇa.
The cries of the blue jay, the porcupine, the proclamation of "Auspicious Day," and the sounds of the bell and conch are auspicious when occurring in water.
One who is domestic should not be accepted if he dwells in the forest, nor one who is wild if he resides in a village;
one who roams by day should not be accepted at night, nor one who roams by night during the day.
Intoxicated birds separated by a river should never be caught under any circumstances.
The red deer, the goat, the wild sheep, the kuraṅga, the camel, the deer, and the rabbit are known to be fruitless in the winter; likewise, the crow and the cuckoo are barren during that season.
But in the month of Bhādrapada, boars, wolves, and the like are not to be taken; in the autumn, aquatic creatures, goats, and krauñca birds; and in Śrāvaṇa, elephants and cātaka birds.
In the winter season, tigers, bears, monkeys, leopards, buffaloes, along with reptiles, are to be known as fruitless; likewise, all children and non-human beings are [fruitless].
Situated in three divisions between the directions of Indra (East) and Agni (Southeast), the treasurers, fire-attendants, and those engaged in asceticism are stationed clockwise.
An artisan, a mendicant, a naked woman, and those situated between the southern and southeastern directions;
furthermore, beyond that, those who rely on the dharma of outcasts and cowherds.
Between the directions of Nairṛti and Varuṇa are women, midwives, and thieves;
between Vāyu and Paścima are the wielder of the Śakti, fowlers, and the violent.
After that, there are the poison-destroyer, the cow-owner, and the master of illusions;
then the wealthy man, the physician, and after him the garland-maker.
The Vaiṣṇava and the Caraka, who is devoted to the protection of horses—
thus the thirty-two divisions have been declared along with the directions of the east.
The king, the prince, the leader, the messenger, the guild-leader, the spy, the twice-born,
and the elephant-keeper— these, starting from the east, are the Kṣatriyas and others situated in the four directions.
Whether one is walking or standing, in whichever direction an omen bird cries out while situated there, a meeting with someone from that same direction is to be predicted.
Vowels that are auspicious, peaceful, joyful, and full of natural vitality are not desired [as defective].
A sow and a cuckoo, as well as those with masculine names, [are auspicious] on the left.

The female (strī), the bhasa, the bhaṣaka, the kapi, the śrīkarṇa, the chitkara, the peacock (śikhin), the śrīkaṇṭha, the pippīka, the ruru deer, and the hawk (śyena) are auspicious when on the right.
Accompanied by drums and musical instruments, they proceed like men; other auspicious sounds are like those of women.
The *grāmas* of Madhyama and Ṣaḍja, as well as Gāndhāra, are auspicious;
the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, Gāndhāra, and Ṛṣabha are beneficial.
Among those seen uttering cries, the peacock, the partridge, and the peacock-pheasant are auspicious;
the mongoose and the blue jay are also fortunate; however, the chameleon portends evil when seen in front.
The mention of the *jāhaka*, the hare, the boar, and the monitor lizard is auspicious;
however, the hearing or sight of the cries of monkeys and bears is not desired, as it is unfavorable.
Ojas has declared that wild animals, mongooses, and birds are auspicious when moving clockwise;
however, Bhṛgu says that the blue jay and the mongoose are auspicious when moving counter-clockwise in the afternoon.
The *chitkara*, the *kūṭapūrī*,
and the *pirilī* are auspicious when occurring on the right side during the day; however, fanged animals and reptiles are always praised when they appear on the left.

If the horse is excellent and dark-colored, there will be corpses in the east and meat in the south; if it has a bulbous root-like protuberance, there will be curd in the west, and in the north, cows, Brahmins, and virtuous men.
A webbed foot and webbed toes are not desired; in the east and south, there are weapons and blows;
in the west, liquor and eunuchs; and in the north, wicked people, seats, and plows.

In matters of action, attachment, battles, entering [a city], and searching for what is lost, one should employ a vehicle that moves in reverse; the specific details regarding this are now being stated.
During the day, deer, ruru-deer, and monkeys are to be caught as if on a journey;
however, during the first part of the day, blue jays, vañjula-birds, and cocks are to be caught.
In the latter part of the night, the Naptṛ, Kokūka, and Piṅgalā—
all of them being reversed— are to be understood as the women among caravans.
During an audience with the king, as well as upon entering [his presence], one should observe the same rules as when setting out on a journey;
likewise when entering mountains or forests, and when plunging into rivers.
Those two [planets] which are auspicious when situated on the left and right are considered harmful when they are in front or behind;
when blazing, they bring destruction to the traveler, being designated as "praigha."
But those two birds themselves, with their cries and movements calmed according to their respective portions,
are known as the "Bird-Door" for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
However, some maintain that there is a "bird-gate" (śakunadvāra) formed by birds of a single species situated on both sides, exhibiting peaceful movements and uttering auspicious cries.
If one person dismisses [the guest] while another opposes it, that conflict is inauspicious for the traveler; or rather, whichever side is more powerful should be followed.
Having first been in the state of entry, one should then become one of departure;
it declares success through ease in the case of entry, and by the opposite in the case of departure.
If, after first flying away, that very same bird returns and obstructs [the traveler],
it foretells death, conflict, or disease for the enemy of the one who travels.
Birds flying to the left are ominous and portend danger;
a bird that is ominous at the commencement of an undertaking brings fear at its conclusion.
The lunar day (tithi), wind (vāyu), the sun (arka), the asterism (bha), the position (sthāna), and the activity (ceṣṭā) are, respectively, "blazing" (dīpta).
They bring about fear for wealth, the army, strength, the body, desired actions, and undertakings.
When [the quarters] are resonant with the sound of clouds, there is danger from the wind;
when they are blazing at both twilights, they portend the fear arising from weapons.
Those situated on funeral pyres, hair, or skulls bring death, bondage, and slaughter;
those situated on thorny wood or ashes bring quarrels, exhaustion, and suffering.
Ominous birds situated on worthless stones cause either failure or fear; however, those that are calm produce only remediable results.
One should know that those two which cause the removal [of obstacles] and the bringing [of results] bestow both failure and success;
if one cries out from one's place, it indicates a journey, but otherwise, it portends arrival.
Quarrels occur when [the planets] are strong by tone (*svara*), and conflict occurs when they are strong by position (*sthāna*). Making a high sound at first and then a low one later causes harm.

If a blazing [fire] cries out while situated in a single place, it causes the destruction of a village within seven days; for cities, regions, and kings, [destruction occurs] after six months, half a year, or a full year, respectively.
All of them will be creators of famine, devouring the flesh of their own kind;
entering into sexual union with other species, they will be destroyers of the land,
except for the arising of offspring from humans through intercourse with animals.
Bondage, injury, and death (or fear) occur through [planets] situated in the feet, thighs, and head;
likewise, the seizure of wealth, loss, and wounds occur through those in the waist, flesh, food, and so forth.
Upon seeing Bhāradvāja, one obtains desired food or milk products;
for a blue jay with a full mouth, there is great gain when it circles to the right.
A *kapiñjala* bird moving to the left or right is excellent, as is one in front;
a *tittiri* bird is excellent behind, while in all other positions it is censured.
A bull bellowing in a favorable direction, as well as a cow and a buffalo, are auspicious;
however, a donkey standing upon the chest portends the prohibition of travel.
An owl on the left is auspicious, as is a cuckoo on the right;
both the *śarkarī* and the peacock are always praised when situated on the right.
Wolves, jackals, tigers, cats, donkeys, dogs,
and deer should be understood as bringing wealth when they appear on the left and on the right.
An empty water-jar and a favorable [jackal] are auspicious for one seeking water who wishes to set out;
they are especially so for those engaged in the science of thievery or in trade.
Chapter 24: The Howling of the Jackal (Śivāruta)
When worshipped from behind, the jackal that is peaceful, auspicious, devoid of flesh and bones,
and possesses a fierce sound and great brilliance, is honored for cruel rites.
A jackal howling in the northeast is auspicious; one that is calm is praised everywhere and honored.
However, if it smokes or faces the observer, it destroys the lords of the directions, even when its own voice is resonant.
The king, the prince, the leader, the messenger, the merchant, the spy, the twice-born,
and the elephant-keeper— these, starting from the east, are the Kṣatriyas and others situated in the four directions.
If [the planet] is inauspicious and blazing in all directions, it is especially inauspicious during the day.
In a pure army, a jackal that circles to the right is auspicious, whereas one facing the east is distressing.
"Go!"—this proclaims the fear of fire; "Ṭāṭa!"—this is impelled by death. "Fie! Fie! I confess my evil deed"—this is the flaming confession that destroys [the transgression].
Some do not at all describe its own flame as being fierce;
for its flame from the mouth is by nature like the fire of the sun and other such sources.
A cry resembling that of another animal in the southern quarter portends the death by hanging; likewise,
a cry resembling that of a water-dweller in the western quarter foretells death in the waters.
Hearing the cry of the *akṣobhya* bird is desired; it brings the acquisition of wealth and the arrival of loved ones.

From agitation [of this bird], there is a breach among the leaders and a lack of prosperity for vehicles. This result holds until the seventh [cry]; beyond that, the cry is not to be taken into account.
In the south, the result is the reverse of that, occurring from the fifth or sixth cry.
That jackal which causes horripilation in men and the discharge of dung and urine in horses,
and produces terror by its howling, does not bestow auspiciousness.
When a female jackal has become silent after responding to the sounds of men, elephants, or horses, she bestows auspiciousness upon the army or the city.
[Chapter 25: The Omens of Crows]
In the month of Vaiśākha, a nest found on a tree that is free from harm is auspicious;
however, its appearance on anthills, sacred shrines, granaries, houses, and the like portends trouble for the region.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, crows with two, three, or four young bring good fortune;
however, those that are reddish-brown, white, or variegated in color portend thieves, fire, and death.
If crows scatter their eggs, there will be both famine and pestilence;
or if the young birds are deformed, or if they are entirely absent.
Whatever object a crow carries away or brings forward in front of one should be understood as indicating the loss of that object; if it is gold or yellow in color, one should predict its recovery.
One who deposits a burnt red substance in another's house is considered an arsonist;
likewise, one who places grass, ashes, bones, or hair upon someone's bed brings about the death of that owner.

If they appear in the sky ahead of the army, there is danger from wind; if they move in a circle to the left, it portends one's own defeat, and if to the right, the emergence of danger from the enemy.

There will be internal dissension among those engaged in improper acts; there will be obstruction for those stationed in a circular formation; there will be assault by groups, and the enemy will increase while remaining fearless.
One should declare the death of its master; there shall be honor if it is worshipped.
Carrying wood, rope, bone, pithless things, hair, and thorns, he cries out,
terrifying [beings] with wild beasts, snakes, disease, weapons, fire, and thieves.

If [the planet] is situated in the divisions of the army components, there is war; if it causes its own sub-division to be scratched, it brings about plunder. Moving through the night, it leads to destruction; if it plunders the grain, it causes famine.
A crow standing on the left side is excellent, as is one moving from the right to the left;
a crow on both sides is also auspicious when its movement is favorable to the journey.
A crow equal in height to the traveler’s ear is auspicious, but it does not bring about the fulfillment of one's purpose.
Moving from left to right is not desired; likewise, one that moves equally or against the direction of travel is not auspicious.
A crow crying out loudly in front of one's side, or shaking its wings, portends fear; likewise, it is an omen of misfortune if it approaches toward the chest or makes physical contact.
A crow with one foot, flapping its wings, or one that drops excrement while swooping down;
or one that cries out while riding upon the backs of donkeys or pigs—these portend death or imprisonment.
A crow perched atop a boar whose body is smeared with mud is commended for a traveler,
whether it remains silent or even caws.
One who provides milk products from a cow-pen containing milk-yielding trees becomes a giver of dairy;
one who cuts leaves becomes a giver of food; and by pounding water, one becomes a giver of drink.
Chapter 26: [The Signs of] Dogs.

If a dog urinates upon men, horses, sunshades, elephants, weapons, banners, or bodies for the sake of victory, it is inauspicious; likewise, wandering about in fear without cause, barking while facing [the owner], or scratching the ground, it is not auspicious.
If dogs bark loudly or emit a piteous cry upon seeing the sun, or if they yawn with their teeth bared, these are not auspicious; likewise, shaking themselves during departures is unfavorable.
A dog with a full mouth, one that sniffs, one that moves clockwise, and one that engages in mating in the natural direction are auspicious at the time of departure.
It is also favorable when a dog scratches its own head with its hind legs.
(Chapter 27: Auspicious and Inauspicious Signs)
White mustard seeds, a mirror, milk, and collyrium; a bound animal, a single fire, and jars filled with meat;
curd, honey, ghee, yellow pigment, and young maidens; banners, gold, lotuses, an auspicious throne, and a conch shell;
a white bull, flowers, garments, fish, flocks of birds, trustworthy people, and those dressed in beautiful attire.
Blazing firebrands, fruits, unbroken grains, parched rice, and edible foods; elephants, clay drums, goads, chowries, and weapons;
and various kinds of jewels, foremost among them emeralds, rubies, sapphires, and crystals.
Whether auspicious signs are produced spontaneously or recounted without effort,
he conquers the entire earth by worshipping them through their seizure, sight, touch, and hearing.
Mud, charcoal, molasses, snakes, hides, and dung; those afflicted by disease;

wind, madness, the dull-witted, and fuel; grass, husks, hunger, emaciation, buttermilk, and wine; shaven heads, anointed bodies, loose hair, the fallen, and those wearing saffron robes—these are inauspicious.

One should proceed along a path where sharp-sounding drums, mṛdaṅgas, conchs, bherīs, and paṇavas resound; where the tops of gateways are adorned with banners and arches; where the dust is laid by an abundance of flowers and water; and where the people are fragrant and well-attired.
(Chapter 28: Auspicious Omens such as Banners, Parasols, and the Like)

If, during the departure of men from the earth, there is a collision of banners, parasols, and weapons; or if, as they rise up, these objects reach the sky and then fall back together, it portends the destruction of the king. Or if there appear ringworm, catarrh, scabies, diseases of the ears or eyes, or the eruption of pustules.
Generally, when either the commander of the army or the king is the leader, know that to be the cause of danger to the monarch.
Likewise, sounds such as "yātu," "āgaccha," "tiṣṭha," "praviśa," "sthira," and so forth, are not desired.
One should know that if a primary omen occurs on any given day, the result of the task undertaken that very day will be certain; thus these [omens] are to be considered.
However, at the time of beginning a journey or entering a place, they hold that a sneeze occurring then is never auspicious.
Some say that the cry of a bird beyond the distance of one *krośa* is fruitless;
in that case, if the first omen is unfavorable, the king should perform five or six *prāṇāyāmas*,
and likewise sixteen if the second is inauspicious.
If the third [alternative] is undesirable, one should return from there to one's own abode.
Having thoroughly examined the opinions of the sages, Varāhamihira has set forth this instruction on omens (*śakuna*) by way of summary.
Whatever has not been stated here—either for fear of excessive length in the book or because it was unknown to him—should be considered from what has been said by others as well.
Chapter 29: On Entering a Dwelling (*niveśa*).
A dwelling place that is smooth, firm, fragrant with shrubs and creepers, scented, and where the water flows clockwise is auspicious.
That which possesses the opposite qualities, and which is crowded with hair, gravel, bones, anthills, thorns, and *vibhītaka* trees, is not desired.
Having gone home, he should remain among the preceptors of the gods, the twice-born, the virtuous, friends, sacred fords, histories, and stories of victory and merit.
Or, having slain an animal made from an enemy's house during an undertaking, he should cast it [into the fire], or else fashion an image of him out of food.
Regarding one who has resided in a single place, Atri, Gautama, and Cyavana have declared that after three,
five, or seven days, one should again join him with the auspicious [lunar mansion].
Those who are experts in the science of *horā* say that this is incorrect;
for a journey is completed only upon the attainment of the fruits of one's desired object.
[Chapter 30: On the Attack]

One who is impatient, harsh in speech, whose servants are disaffected, and who goes to the wives of others; one who is greedy, without allies, addicted to vice, ungrateful, and a breaker of established order—such a king has his kingdom destroyed by his own taxes.

One who betrays trust, is under the sway of anger, cruel, base, negligent, and lacking in extensive learning; and one who is afflicted by disturbances arising from the heavens, the atmosphere, or the earth—he indeed is one devoid of fortune.
Therefore, when a king of opposite qualities attacks such an enemy, that enemy—though great—quickly meets with destruction, its strength consumed like a tree gnawed by woodworms.
Chapter 31: The Army, Wind, Rain, Meteors, Earthquakes, Thunder, and Twilight.
An army whose excellent men are hostile, whose prowess has faded, whose warriors are devoid of purity and deprived of their finest elephants,
and which is beset by portents and natural reversals, quickly falls under the power of the enemy, afflicted by grief.
"By the grace of the gods and the twice-born, we shall undoubtedly overcome the enemy force in battle.
When such a proclamation regarding one's strength arises among the people, even a small army destroys an enemy of vast power.

A wind that is foul-smelling, born from the discharge of elephants, accompanied by whirlwinds and rising clods of earth, brings misfortune to one on a journey; whereas a wind that is refreshing, fragrant, moving clockwise,
and pleasant to the taste brings success.
A mass of clouds that is broad, moving with the wind, glossy, and resembling young mountains, cities, desirable objects, or living beings;
or one that stands on both sides or behind [the king], brings victory to the lord of men at the time of his departure. Any other kind is not auspicious.
When beings reviled as *piśācas*, diverse in form, having the appearance of flesh-eating deer, and harsh;
or when they emit thunderbolts, blood, or stones—people say that such portents quickly bring about the fear of a powerful force.

When clouds are seen in the sky for the sake of battle— pouring down copiously, reddened with blood, accompanied by rainbows, making harsh and rough sounds, and possessing various wonderful forms suitable for warfare.

Rain occurring out of season within seven days causes fear for the army; some, however, honor a journey when it is initiated by dark clouds. When there are variegated clouds, there is the death of the commander-in-chief; when the clouds are yellow, there is disease.
If [the wind] is hot, there will be rain before long; if it is accompanied by clouds, destruction follows.
If it is on the left side, it destroys vehicles; if otherwise, it destroys women.
When situated in the form of a cage, it destroys the lord of the entire army from all sides.
A bow belonging to Indra that is straight, unbroken, radiant, thick, long,
and desirable— resounding, consecrated with water from a ritual jar, and like a turbulent ocean— is for the sake of victory.
A slender, long, and hanging flash of lightning, devoid of thunder from a cloud, is auspicious;
likewise, a thunderbolt is favorable when it does not strike nearby, and the sound of its fall is auspicious if it comes from the right.
If the Sun and Moon are in the ascendant, a meteor falling while striking them portends harm to the citizens; however, such meteors and planets would destroy the enemies of the traveler.
A meteor that is well-formed or gathered in the Dhruva constellation is auspicious for the traveler; any other that is smoky or dark-red is not desired.
It destroys the king, the citizens, the subjects, the servants, the lotuses, the thieves, and the twice-born;
it proceeds gradually from the beginning of the day through the *kāṣṭhā*, and wherever there is a sound of thunder on the earth.
A twilight that is praised, resonant with the cries of peaceful birds and deer, gentle, and where the forests are lush, brings prosperity;
however, one that is covered in dust, harsh, or resembles the color of blood, portends the destruction of the realm.
(Chapter 32: Portents)

An aureole around the sun and moon, occurring together with planets belonging to the faction of one's enemies, brings victory if it is glossy and unbroken; however, it brings misfortune if it consists of many circles.
A contrary wind that is excessive is undesirable, whereas one that is clockwise is desirable.
Likewise, mist and falling dust are beneficial when they are moist and move in a clockwise direction.
A Gandharvanagara (phantom city) omen destroys, in sequence, first the sovereign of the earth,
then the lord of the army, the crown prince, and the domestic priest.
White and so forth [are the omens] for Brahmins and the other castes; those of mixed caste appear in the intermediate directions.
During a journey, these occurring in a clockwise direction bring victory; otherwise, they are not desired.
The burning of the quarters, when occurring in a clockwise direction, brings victory;
however, if it occurs in a hollow or an elevated place, it portends the king's death, whereas by the reverse of this, it leads to victory.
If there is a flow of ghee, water, or milk, or if they fall from a tree, there will be their destruction;
if it is oil, there is ruin for the leaders; and if it is blood, there is danger from weapons.
If [the flower] is moistened with liquor, there will be mutual dissension; if it flows out as curd, there will be illness and fear.
If another flower arises from a flower, one should predict the arrival of a foreign army.

If there is excessive drying up of abundant water, or if blood flows from a well that has been filled with it, these portend the death of the king within half a year; if the flow becomes diminished, there will be the arrival of an enemy.

During rain, lightning, and thunder in a cloudless sky, or when there is a reversal of the states of moving and stationary objects, and during the appearance of a meteor during the day, the people suffer along with their kings.
If these [omens] persist for seven days, rain shall destroy the king;
furthermore, if fire fails to ignite, disease will soon arise among men.
There will be suffering for the kingdom after six months due to the reversal of heat and cold;
and in the eighth month, there will be the end of the king if there is a shrieking among the beasts and birds.
When beings of cities and forests resort to forests and cities respectively,
and when the rains are excessive, causing distress to the realm, there is destruction of the principal people.
Furthermore, in the case of an earthquake, one should declare the destruction of the region within three months.
In the sixth month, there will be the slaughter of cattle, elephants, and horses, or else a reversal that brings about the end of the king;
likewise, there will be the destruction of the country when birds, snakes, and beasts appear [in unnatural abundance].

The death of one’s son or wife, the commands of petty kings, the distress of death caused by the king’s army, internal dissension, loss of position, the ruin of ministers, disease, and the king’s wrath.
At night, a rainbow of white color and the like causes suffering to the twice-born and others;
moreover, it shall soon destroy the preeminent king in whichever direction it appears.
The cries of deer, cattle, donkeys, horses, and elephants in the sky portend danger before long;
likewise, the falling of the banner and the archway of the Lord of the Gods produces this very same result for kings.
[Chapter 33] Regarding the capture of cities and fortresses:
When the malefic planets are pure and situated in the twelfth, the four angles (kendras), or the eighth house, while the benefics are in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses;

or when Jupiter—the preceptor of the gods—or Venus—the worshipful one of the Daityas—is placed in the ascendant or an angle; and when the sign at the time of birth (udaya) and the sign occupied by the lord of the year are auspicious, there is the successful attainment of the fruits of all undertakings for the doer.
If the lord of the third house is strong and has a stable rising sign, one should build a fine dwelling or enter upon a new undertaking.
On a day when a cruel [ascendant] rises, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the Riktā lunar days, at the ends of the seasons, or during the Vaidhṛti yoga;
and under sharp and fierce asterisms, acts involving fire, poison, or violence achieve success during the dark fortnight.
When Ketu, an ulkā, Saturn, Rāhu, Kīlaka, or Mars enter the solar or lunar disc, or if a partial halo (pariveṣa) of the sun or moon is seen in a particular direction;
or if jackals, dogs, snakes, ants, rabbits, deer, crows, and the like appear in the city— 33.3–34ab.
Or if they enter the army from a certain direction, then the weapons shall strike the city from that same direction.
If Rāhu or Ketu is in the mansion of Pātāla, one should predict the cessation of water and the falling of *sāla* trees in the city.
If Mars is situated in the seventh house (*jāmitra*) or in its own division (*aṃśaka*), and is aspected by the Moon’s son [Saturn], fire must be declared.
Chapter 34: *Jayottara* (Victory)
Due to the falling of meteors, forest fires, blood, dust, and showers of stones; due to portents such as thunderclaps and earthquakes;
and due to beasts and birds emitting fierce cries at the conclusion of battle—even upon victory, it is not well for the king.
When the beasts and birds are auspicious, the gentle breeze brings refreshment,
the planets have clear rays, and the quarters of the sky are free from dust;
and when no other portentous anomaly occurs at the conclusion of the victory—
At that time, the king enjoys his realm without thorns;
he who has performed the marriage, an untimely festival, and the consecration of his son returns unhindered from his departure on those festive days.

Upon reaching the territory and cities of an enemy, a ruler of the earth should not seize the property of virtuous deities and the twice-born, nor should he obstruct their families, subjects, or women;
nor should he strike those who are without elephants, horses, or weapons, nor those who are afflicted or terrified.
On an auspicious lunar day, day, and asterism, with his army delighted, he shall bring [the enemy] under his control.
Having approached his own domain,
the lord of men should offer oblations and additional prayers according to the prescribed ritual to the deities of the first group, beginning with the Asuras and Bhūtas.

Thus, that lord of men who acts according to the instructions of those who know the movements of the celestial bodies shall, in no long time, attain sovereignty over the entire circle of kings, just as Purandara does in heaven. E6.
End of the *Bṛhadyātrā*.
